title: Southern Gold Coast cocoa roads and lorry enterprise: local initiative with unequal entry
period: Main transport episode 1910s–1931; explicitly separate land/labour context from the 1890s–1930s
summary: African farmers, chiefs and owner-drivers supplied part of the road/lorry system alongside state infrastructure. Land rights, credit, hired migration and coercion differentiated entry and burdens.

stages.invention: Imported motor vehicles; no local vehicle-invention claim.
stages.feasibility: Working lorry haulage and named feeder-road construction projects are documented.
stages.deployment: Chiefs contracted roads or worked with commissioners; smaller African operators joined earlier fleets.
stages.diffusion: Historical descriptions of owner-driver expansion and quoted modal freight shares, not an ownership adoption rate.
stages.scaling: Road and vehicle growth supported additional routes; finance, vehicle upkeep and road maintenance remained material.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Head-loading commonly persisted from farms to local markets; not all actors could enter farming or vehicle ownership.
stages.displacement/reversal: Some direct lorry haulage competed with rail after an earlier complementary phase; no universal or permanent railway displacement claim.

counterevidence: State investment, imported vehicles, road standards and coercive labour coexist with African enterprise; success does not measure consent or equal welfare.

episode.technology_configuration: Southern feeder/trade roads, motor lorries and rail interchanges serving cocoa; land and labour arrangements are explicitly contextual subepisodes, not a common operator cohort.
episode.task: Move cocoa and people to stations, markets or ports and develop cultivable land; official fiscal and administrative purposes need not match every user’s interests.
episode.population: Named road sponsors, chiefs, land-buying groups, lorry owner-drivers and historical southern crop/transport aggregates; land/labour context concerns different farmer and worker groups.
episode.interval: Transport 1910s–1931, with specific 1927–28 operator report and 1922–23/1930–31 freight shares; land and farm-labour context 1890s–1930s.
contemporary_alternatives: rail long hauls with lorry feeders
buying or leasing land under locally different rules
hired work or own farming where accessible
episode.adoption_measure: Named deployments, contemporary reports of owner-drivers and modal cocoa export shares inherited through Austin. No population denominator for lorry ownership, failed entry, driver income or local consent.
episode.observation_limits: Official and scholarly accounts are selected and partly share sources. Modal shares and route availability differ by period; land and worker populations cannot be pooled with owner-drivers.

actors.chooser: Growers and village groups requested some connections; chiefs contracted or negotiated projects and controlled some land rights; owner-drivers chose vehicles/routes subject to finance; colonial officers set public investment and regulation.
actors.payer: Owners or hire-purchase creditors financed vehicles; growers/groups financed some land and roads; chiefs, public funds and uncompensated or compelled labour supplied other resources. Contract incidence is incompletely known.
actors.operator_maintainer: Owner-drivers and employed drivers, repair workers, road gangs and community labour; cocoa cultivation used self/family, hired migrant and in earlier Ashanti also coerced labour.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Road labourers, enslaved people/pawns in the early farm-building context, families, land users and people exposed to road changes; not the same population as enterprise owners.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Enterprise initiative is documented for named actors. Enslaved/pawned and corvée labour had coercive constraints; chiefs could require road work. Hired migrants’ choices depended on land, wages and alternative employment. Consent of every road contributor or landholder is not demonstrated.

labour.tasks: Driving, repair, route finding, loading and continuing head-loading; road construction and recurring maintenance; crop cultivation by multiple paid/unpaid/coerced arrangements.
labour.entry_barriers: Vehicle finance, upkeep and operating capability; land access and crop maturation; different tenure and local stranger status. Hire-purchase terms, default and complete skills barriers are not reconstructed.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Chiefly fleets, small owner-drivers, landholders, land-buying groups, hired migrants and obligated workers controlled different assets and choices; cash overheads can omit owner/family hours and public road costs.
labour.transition: Reports show expanding owner-driving and changing farm labour relations, not linked careers from carriers or coerced workers to profitable transport enterprise.
labour.distribution: Land access differed across regions/status; Austin describes regional and gender inequalities. Contemporary accounts of owner profits cannot establish net worker returns or universal benefit.
labour.evidence_limit: No net employment balance, representative household welfare, default distribution or individual consent panel. No inference that local ownership guarantees voluntary supply-chain labour.

title: Northern public roads: changing paid recruitment beside persistent and disputed compulsion
region: Northern Territories of the Gold Coast
period: 1925–1937, with earlier construction context and explicitly separate PWD/political-road subepisodes
outcome: partial shift to paid voluntary work
summary: PWD recruitment changed in some places before convention ratification, while other road obligations persisted. Administrative strategies, worker alternatives, funding and local dissent interacted; scholarship differs on transition breadth.

stages.invention: No road-technology invention; the change concerns recruitment and maintenance organization.
stages.feasibility: Both compulsory service and hired gangs performed road tasks, with reported quality and recruitment problems.
stages.deployment: Makongo bargaining in 1925 and Savelugu recruitment instruction in June 1930 identify particular changes before ratification.
stages.diffusion: Pont Cháfer reconstructs other local shifts; Kunkel documents continuing mechanisms of compulsion. No common labour-days denominator.
stages.scaling: Increasing traffic and year-round maintenance strained short obligatory service; budgets and worker supply mattered.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Residual compulsory cleaning/weeding persisted even on PWD roads; political-road regimes were heterogeneous.
stages.displacement/reversal: Some recruitment shifted toward voluntary paid gangs, without a single verified end date for all compelled road tasks.

counterevidence: Payment is not proof of free recruitment; pre-ratification changes do not exclude earlier external pressure; planned subsidy and actual payroll are different evidence.

episode.technology_configuration: Subepisode A: paid PWD maintenance/reconstruction around Makongo, Salaga and Savelugu. Subepisode B: political/public roads maintained through chiefs and district authorities in the 1930s.
episode.task: Keep motor routes usable, including rainy-season repairs; reduce recruitment costs or coercion depending on the actor.
episode.population: PWD applicants/recruits, chiefs and local officers in cited disputes; separate communities and administrative units under political-road arrangements. These are not one tracked cohort.
episode.interval: Main observations 1925, June 1930 and mid/late 1930s; construction before 1925 is context.
contemporary_alternatives: paid voluntary recruitment at a sufficiently attractive offer
reduced maintained mileage or deteriorating roads
episode.adoption_measure: Dated disputes, recruitment instructions, wage comparisons, budget assumptions and reported expenditures; no estimated share of workers or days free from coercion.
episode.observation_limits: Original archives mediated through scholarship; PWD roads were a minority of northern mileage and different tasks had different rules. Kunkel/Pont Cháfer disagree on interpretation and extent.

actors.chooser: PWD and colonial authorities commissioned work; chiefs and district/provincial officers negotiated or enforced recruitment; workers supplied or withheld labour within uneven constraints.
actors.payer: PWD/public budgets, later grants and local treasuries; compelled workers and their households also bore time and subsistence costs. Subsidy assumptions do not establish actual payment.
actors.operator_maintainer: Recruited road workers, hired gangs and residents obliged to weed or clean; skilled supervisors and road engineers where available.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers subject to recruitment or residual duties, households losing farm time, communities taxed or passed by, and road users facing deterioration.
actors.ability_to_refuse: A June 1930 Savelugu instruction rejects forced PWD supply and advertises paid work; earlier desertion could be punished. Residual tasks and political-road practices retained coercive powers. No universal consent inference from wages.

labour.tasks: Construction/maintenance, drainage, repair, cleaning and weeding; motor traffic altered timing and quality demands.
labour.entry_barriers: Recruitment authority, acceptable wages and food costs, agricultural calendar, location and alternative southern employment; exact skills/selection distribution unavailable.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Workers’ alternatives and chiefs’ protests could change terms, while public authorities retained coercive and fiscal powers. Chiefs were neither uniform intermediaries nor uniformly autonomous protectors.
labour.transition: Specific changes precede 1931 ratification; further administrative and financing changes occurred during the 1930s. Different tasks did not change simultaneously.
labour.distribution: Freedom from compelled supply could improve for particular recruits while the Depression weakened southern earnings; no total welfare or gender-distribution estimate.
labour.evidence_limit: No road-linked panel of contracts, sanctions, payments and hours; no aggregate compulsory-work percentage or universal abolition date.

title: Krachi–Salaga–Kpandai feeder roads: farmer initiative and maintenance tied to lorry use
period: 1928–1945, with separately identified later oral context
summary: Named village initiatives sought feeder roads and outside technical resources; a reported 1945 interruption of exports coincided with deterioration of one route, showing a conditional maintenance problem.

stages.invention: No road or vehicle invention claim.
stages.feasibility: Cleared routes required bridges, culverts, suitable surfaces and lorry service to work as motor connections.
stages.deployment: Bajamse sought route alignment in 1928; other named village connections and subsequent grants are recorded in 1937.
stages.diffusion: Selected connections expanded by 1945 in the source; no complete denominator of villages, road users or failed requests.
stages.scaling: Villagers’ labour and local knowledge were combined with scarce materials, skilled construction and administrative assistance.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Assistance and participation were uneven; later oral examples are not backdated as evidence for every interwar village.
stages.displacement/reversal: Bladjai’s road reportedly deteriorated when fuel shortages stopped exports in April 1945; duration and eventual recovery not established here.

counterevidence: Some routes in the same area had earlier coercive origins; a local chief’s petition does not prove all-household consent. Fuel disruption has potential confounders.

episode.technology_configuration: Farmer/village feeder connections to larger roads and lorry-based food marketing, with materials and skilled work sought from officials/native authorities.
episode.task: Connect villages to lorry routes and southern food markets; maintain usable passage when marketing continues.
episode.population: Named village initiatives and reported Bladjai maintenance sequence; later interview populations are supplementary context, not the same observed 1928 cohort.
episode.interval: 1928 Bajamse request; 1937 connections/grants; expansion and April 1945 Bladjai interruption. Later oral accounts are identified as later, without assigning their undated details to this interval.
episode.adoption_measure: Dated petitions, reported connections/grants and one qualitative maintenance reversal; no ownership, traffic, household benefit or participation-rate denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Selected administrative entries and later oral history; no systematic failed-project sample, unobserved household disagreement or weather-adjusted comparison.

actors.chooser: Farmers and villagers initiated particular requests; chiefs or other representatives negotiated; officials/native authorities selected assistance and expenditure.
actors.payer: Villagers supplied labour and some local resources; administrative grants, tools, materials and skilled work supplied other inputs. Household burden shares unknown.
actors.operator_maintainer: Local road workers and hired specialists where obtained; lorry operators transported produce and farmers sometimes paid freight.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Households contributing labour or unable to use the road, adjacent land users and people whose request was denied; their separate outcomes are poorly recorded.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Requests and village initiatives support local demand, but do not establish each resident’s consent. Later evidence of weak chiefs or failed collective participation informs interpretation without proving identical conditions in every interwar village.

labour.tasks: Clearing and recurring upkeep, materials gathering and seeking skilled bridge/culvert work, agricultural marketing and haulage.
labour.entry_barriers: Cost of bringing materials and attracting skilled workers, access to grants and lorry service/fuel; unequal assistance documented qualitatively.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Villagers could negotiate labour for assistance; officials controlled some technical/fiscal resources. Ownership of produce or lorry service remained distinct from performing road labour.
labour.transition: Route-specific creation and decline rather than tracked occupational mobility. 1945 reversal does not establish permanent abandonment.
labour.distribution: Potentially useful market access does not establish equal net benefit; full farm, maintenance, freight and household accounts absent.
labour.evidence_limit: No demonstrated worker-income gain or universal voluntariness; a qualitative export interruption does not identify a maintenance elasticity.
